H1.text: At the college fest, Aarav whispers into a microphone.

H2.text: The speakers boom across the whole ground.

H3.text: Walking home, a street lamp switches on by itself at dusk.

H4.text: Two very different jobs. One tiny part does both. A transistor.

P1.text: Think of a water tap on a big pipe.

P2.text: A small twist of the handle controls a big flow of water.

P3.text: Close it fully, and no water flows. Open it fully, and you get full flow.

P4.text: Wiggle the handle a little, and the big flow wiggles too.

P5.text: A transistor is a tap for current. It has three legs.

P6.text: The base is the handle. A tiny current goes in here.

P7.text: The collector is where the big current comes in.

P8.text: The emitter is where both currents leave together.

P9.text: A small base current controls a big collector current. That is the whole trick.

S1.text: Let's build the switch on the breadboard.

S2.text: A five volt supply, a lamp, and an n p n transistor.

S3.text: A resistor feeds the base from an input switch.

S4.text: Input at zero volts. No base current flows.

S5.text: So no collector current either. The lamp stays off. This is called cut off.

S6.text: Now flip the input to five volts. A small base current flows.

S7.text: The tap opens fully. Electrons rush through, and the lamp lights up.

S8.text: This fully on state is called saturation. The transistor acts like a closed switch.

S9.text: Watch the scope. When the input goes high, the output goes low.

S10.text: The output is taken across the transistor. So this switch also flips the signal.

M1.text: Now the amplifier. We give the base a small, steady current.

M2.text: The tap is now half open. The lamp glows half bright.

M3.text: Then we add a tiny wave from a microphone, just ten millivolts.

M4.text: The base current wiggles a little. The collector current wiggles a lot.

M5.text: Watch the scope. The output wave is a hundred times bigger.

M6.text: But look closely. When the input goes up, the output goes down.

M7.text: The output is upside down. We call this one eighty degrees out of phase.

G1.text: So when is it a switch, and when is it an amplifier?

G2.text: Plot the output voltage against the input voltage.

G3.text: Below about zero point seven volts, the base is shut. The output stays high.

G4.text: That flat part is cut off. The switch is off.

G5.text: At a high input, the transistor is fully on. The output is nearly zero.

G6.text: That flat part is saturation. The switch is on.

G7.text: In between is the steep active region. A small input change makes a big output change.

T1.text: A switch at the two ends. An amplifier in the middle.

D1.text: Now the maths, one small step at a time.

D2.text: Both currents leave through the emitter. So I E equals I B plus I C.

D3.text: The collector current is beta times the base current. Beta is the current gain.

D4.text: The output is the supply, minus the drop on the collector resistor.

D5.text: So V out equals V C C, minus I C times R C.

D6.text: Divide the output change by the input change. That is the voltage gain.

D7.text: A V equals minus beta, times R C, divided by R in, the input resistance.

D8.text: Beta has no unit. It is a ratio of two currents. The minus sign means upside down.

W1.text: Worked example. Is the lamp fully on?

W2.text: The supply is five volts. The lamp is one kilo ohm. Beta is one hundred.

W3.text: The input is five volts, through a base resistor of ten kilo ohms.

W4.text: The base current is five minus zero point seven, over ten kilo ohms.

W5.text: That is zero point four three milliamperes.

W6.text: Beta times this asks for forty three milliamperes.

W7.text: But the lamp circuit can carry at most five volts over one kilo ohm. Just five milliamperes.

W8.text: The base asks for more than the circuit can give. So the transistor is saturated. The lamp is fully on.

X2.text: Many students think the amplified output moves in step with the input.

X3.text: In a common emitter amplifier, it does not. The output is one eighty degrees out of phase.

X4.text: And the transistor does not make energy. The extra power comes from the supply.

X5.text: Where is this asked? In P U C and I S C board papers.

X6.text: Draw the circuit, explain the switch and the amplifier, and find the currents and the gain.

Q1.text: Try this. A common emitter amplifier has beta fifty, an input resistance of one kilo ohm, and a collector resistance of five kilo ohms. A ten millivolt signal goes in. What comes out?

A1.text: C. Two point five volts, one eighty degrees out of phase.

A2.text: The voltage gain is beta times R C, divided by R in.

A3.text: Fifty times five, divided by one. That is a gain of two hundred and fifty.

A4.text: Two hundred and fifty times ten millivolts is two point five volts. And the output is upside down.
